newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-JACQUET WANTS MORE AUDACITY FROM HIS FORWARDS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-JACQUET WANTS MORE AUDACITY FROM HIS FORWARDS.

text.p: France closed their World Cup dress rehearsal with two fine examples of finishing, so often a problem area for them, but paradoxically one of the world's best defences was found wanting.
Italy twice came from behind to draw 2-2 in Wednesday's last match of the Tournoi de France, denying the hosts a boost to their World Cup preparations.

The French defence were unable to protect a 2-1 lead in the last 18 minutes, conceding a last-gasp penalty converted by Alessandro Del Piero and reviving the ghost of their failure to reach the 1994 World Cup finals.
In November 1993, France failed to hang on for a draw at home to Bulgaria, giving away a last-minute goal that put their rivals into the U.S. finals in their place.

Coach Aime Jacquet said fatigue at the end of an exhausting season was partly responsible for mistakes in conceding crucial goals in the final minutes against both Italy and England. Alan Shearer gave England a 1-0 win in Montpellier on Saturday when he scored in the 85th minute.
"This match (against Italy) is a resume of the whole tournament," said Jacquet, whose side opened with a promising 1-1 draw with world champions Brazil.
"In our last two matches we let in goals in the last minutes which proves the players no longer had the necessary lucidity and athletic resources at the end of the game."

Just three goals in three games have not eased Jacquet's concerns about his attack even if against Italy the key players directly behind the strikers, Zinedine Zidane and Youri Djorkaeff, scored wonderful goals.
Jacquet tried out six strikers during the Tournoi.

"What is really annoying is that we have formidable firepower but don't use it. We daren't shoot at goal. We wait for the most favourable situation because it's not in our nature to be spontaneous," he said at a news conference on Thursday where he analysed France's performance.
"These matches were not a big satisfaction because they did not allow us to project ourselves into the future," he said.
"Everything was wrong from before (the start). The players were engaged with their clubs. We were unable to make adequate preparations to face such prestigious adversaries."
But it was not all negative for Jacquet, whose team's defeat against England was only their second in his 37 matches in charge.

"The mental (part) is there. The French team are now conscious of their possibilities, of the progress they have to make and the importance of what is at stake," he said almost exactly a year before the start of the 1998 World Cup finals.
"Spirit, a bit of luck and the occasion will allow us to do something important in the World Cup," he said.
